t.archaeological landscape of the first co:
In the hills of southeastern Cuba, between Santiago and Guantánamo, the ruins of old coffee plantations lie hidden in the forest, and they tell a remarkable story. After the slave revolution in Saint-Domingue in the 1790s, which led to the independence of Haiti, many French planters fled to Cuba with their enslaved workers, and they introduced coffee growing on a large scale in the Sierra Maestra foothills. In the nineteenth century, hundreds of cafetales were established, with mansions, drying platforms, mills, aqueducts and slave quarters, using innovative techniques adapted to the steep mountain terrain. The Archaeological Landscape of the First Coffee Plantations in the South-East of Cuba was listed by UNESCO in 2000.

The plantations are a reminder of the wealth created by coffee and of the brutal system of slavery that sustained it.

The landscape is green and mountainous, with tropical forests, coffee bushes in the shade of larger trees, and small villages. The roads in this region are often narrow, steep and in poor condition, with potholes and sometimes unpaved sections, and the climate is hot and humid, with heavy rain in the wet season. The road to the Gran Piedra, from the coast east of Santiago, climbs steeply through the forest with many bends, and the views from the top are spectacular when the clouds lift.

Independent motorcycle travel in Cuba is complicated. Bringing your own bike is difficult, rentals are limited, and fuel shortages have been a serious problem in recent years, with long queues and stations running dry, so plan for uncertainty and carry extra fuel if you can. Guantánamo, about twenty-three kilometres away, and Santiago de Cuba have the most services. Local food includes congrí, rice and black beans cooked together, roast pork, and of course strong Cuban coffee, which you can sometimes buy directly from farmers in the mountains. The people are warm and resourceful, and the music of the region, son, was born in these eastern provinces.
t.la gran piedra@20.0,-75.6:
La Gran Piedra means simply the Great Stone, and that is exactly what waits at the top: an enormous boulder sitting on the crest of the Sierra de la Gran Piedra, over twelve hundred metres above sea level and roughly twenty kilometres east of Santiago de Cuba. You climb several hundred stone steps from the road to reach it, and a metal ladder takes you onto the rock itself. On a clear morning the view runs over forested ridges to the Caribbean on one side and inland across the Sierra Maestra on the other, and people say that on the clearest nights you can see the lights of Jamaica and Haiti.

The mountains here carry a story of migration. After the Haitian Revolution at the end of the eighteenth century, French coffee planters fled to eastern Cuba and established plantations on these cool, misty slopes. The ruins of their estates, with drying floors, water channels and stone houses, are part of the Archaeological Landscape of the First Coffee Plantations in the South-East of Cuba, a World Heritage site. La Isabelica, a restored plantation house a short distance from the summit, is now a museum showing how the estates worked, and it is a short, rough ride or walk from the main road.

The road up is one of the most dramatic climbs in Cuba. It leaves the coast road near Siboney and twists up through tropical forest in a long series of tight, steep bends, with the temperature dropping noticeably as you climb. The surface is broken in places, there are no barriers on some drops, and mist can roll in suddenly, so take it slowly and keep your eyes up. The forest is lush with ferns, giant bamboo and orchids, and there is a botanical garden on the way with tropical flowers.

Practical matters in Cuba need extra care. Fuel can be hard to find and queues long, so fill up in Santiago before you go and carry what you can. There are a few basic facilities near the summit, but do not count on them. The best time to ride is in the dry season, roughly November to April, early in the day before the clouds build. Pack water, a light jacket for the top, and patience, since Cuban roads demand plenty of it.
Up in Carchi, Ecuador's northernmost province, a short stretch of old stone-edged road near San Gabriel is all that is left visible of something enormous. The Qhapaq Ñan, the Inca road system, ran from what is now southern Colombia to central Chile and Argentina, tens of thousands of kilometres of paths, stairways and causeways that tied the empire together. The segment between Mariscal Sucre and El Tambo is one of the pieces listed by UNESCO in 2014 as part of that network. A tambo was a waystation, a place where runners and travellers could rest and resupply, so the name itself tells you what stood here.

The Inca only reached this far north late, a few decades before the Spanish arrived, and the local peoples of the region, among them the Pasto, resisted. Walking even a short bit of the path you notice how it holds a steady line across the slope, built for feet and llamas rather than wheels.

The landscape is high Andean country, roughly between two and a half and three and a half thousand metres, a patchwork of potato and pasture fields climbing into the páramo. North of El Ángel lies an ecological reserve famous for frailejones, the furry-leaved giant rosette plants that look like they were designed for another planet. Weather changes fast: bright sun, then cloud pouring over the ridges, then cold drizzle. Ride with layers and a rain suit you can reach quickly.

The main access is the Pan-American Highway, which in this section is a mix of good wide tarmac and slower winding stretches through towns, with trucks, buses and dogs to keep you alert. The side roads up to the villages can be cobbles or dirt, and they get slippery when wet. San Gabriel, about eleven kilometres away and home to some fifteen thousand people, is where you find fuel, food and a bed; Tulcán, the border city further north, is bigger and has a famously elaborate topiary cemetery that is worth an hour. Order a hot locro de papa, the potato and cheese soup, to warm up after a cold ride, and keep in mind that at this altitude you tire faster than you think.
t.guantanamo@20.2,-75.2:
Most people know Guantánamo for two things: a song and a naval base. The song, Guantanamera, about a peasant girl from Guantánamo, became one of the most famous Cuban tunes in the world, with verses adapted from the poetry of José Martí. The base, leased to the United States since 1903 on the shores of Guantánamo Bay, is a separate, fenced enclave south of the city, and it is not a place you can visit. The city itself, in the far east of Cuba, is a sleepy provincial capital with a grid of low, colourful houses, a central square and a strong musical tradition. It is the birthplace of changüí, a rustic ancestor of son, played with tres guitar, bongos and marímbula.

The province is the most mountainous and least visited in Cuba. To the north, the mountains of Yateras and the Alejandro de Humboldt National Park, a UNESCO site, protect some of the richest rainforests in the Caribbean, with endemic species of plants, frogs and birds. To the west, toward Santiago, the slopes of the Sierra Maestra hold the ruins of French coffee plantations established by refugees from Haiti in the nineteenth century, also listed by UNESCO, and the Gran Piedra, a huge rock on a mountain top, offers views over the sea.

Riding in eastern Cuba is an adventure. The roads are often potholed, with horse carts, cyclists, trucks crammed with people and livestock to dodge, and signposting is poor. The most spectacular road is La Farola, which crosses the mountains from the south coast to Baracoa, with hairpins, steep climbs and views of the forest and the sea. Fuel can be hard to find, with shortages and long queues at stations, so plan carefully and carry extra. The heat is intense, and the rainy season from May to October brings heavy storms and the risk of hurricanes.

Guantánamo, with over two hundred and seventy thousand inhabitants, has basic services, including fuel when available, shops and casas particulares, private guesthouses. Try local dishes such as congrí, rice with black beans, roast pork, and fried plantains. In Baracoa, the cuisine is different, with coconut, cocoa and dishes like cucurucho, a sweet made from coconut, honey and fruit, wrapped in palm leaves.
t.chitarran@0.9,-77.4:
In the high Andes of southern Colombia, near the border with Ecuador, the Inca road network reached its northern limit. The Qhapaq Ñan, as the system is called, stretched from here to central Chile, and a few segments in the department of Nariño are part of the UNESCO listing of 2014. Chitarrán is one of these, a stretch of old road near the villages of Córdoba, Contadero and Iles, in a landscape of green hills, ravines and patchwork fields at altitudes of over two thousand metres.

Nariño is a land of volcanoes, with Cumbal, Chiles and Azufral rising above the plateaus, and of deep canyons cut by rivers such as the Guáitara. Near Ipiales, the border town, the sanctuary of Las Lajas is an extraordinary neo-Gothic church built on a bridge spanning the Guáitara gorge, one of the most remarkable sights in South America. The indigenous Pasto people have lived here for centuries, and the villages have a strong cultural identity, with markets, festivals and crafts. The Carnaval de Negros y Blancos in Pasto, held in early January, is one of the most colourful festivals in Colombia.

The riding in Nariño is spectacular. The Pan-American Highway runs through the region, with long climbs, curves and views over the canyons, and the minor roads to the villages wind through hills and fields, often unpaved. The surface varies, with landslides possible in the rainy season. Altitude and cold weather can be a challenge, with temperatures dropping at night, and fog is common. Traffic includes trucks and buses, and local drivers can be aggressive. Check the security situation before travelling in rural areas.

For fuel, Ipiales and Pupiales are the reliable towns. Food in Nariño includes cuy, roasted guinea pig, a local delicacy, as well as potatoes, corn and hearty soups. Hot drinks such as hervido, a warm fruit drink with aguardiente, help against the cold. The Inca road segment is best explored on foot, with a local guide if possible. Stand on the old stones and look out over the hills; the Inca empire reached this far north just before the Spanish arrived, and the road is a reminder of its astonishing ambition.
t.segment la paz quebrada tupala@0.5,-77.8:
The province of Carchi, at the northern tip of Ecuador, is high, green and cool, a land of potato fields, dairy farms and páramo, the high-altitude grassland of the Andes. The Inca road ran through here on its way north, and the segment between La Paz and the Quebrada Tupala is one of the Ecuadorian sections of the Qhapaq Ñan listed by UNESCO. Near the village of La Paz, a natural cave in the rock, the Gruta de La Paz, has been turned into a shrine to the Virgin, with a church inside the cave, and it draws pilgrims from across the region.

The páramo of El Ángel, a protected reserve to the west, is famous for its frailejones, tall plants with fuzzy leaves and thick trunks that look like something from a fantasy film. They grow only in the high Andes of Colombia, Venezuela and Ecuador, and they store water like sponges, feeding the rivers below. San Gabriel, the nearest larger town, is a market centre for the region, and Pimampiro and El Ángel are smaller towns in the valleys. Tulcán, the provincial capital on the border with Colombia, is known for its cemetery with elaborately clipped topiary.

The riding here is excellent, with a few challenges. The Pan-American Highway runs through Carchi, with curves, climbs and views over the valleys, and the minor roads to villages and reserves wind through hills and páramo, often unpaved. Altitude is high, over three thousand metres in places, and the weather is cold, wet and foggy, with sudden changes. Dress warmly. The surface varies, and landslides are possible in the rainy season. Watch for trucks, buses and livestock.

San Gabriel sorts out fuel and lunch, and Tulcán, further north, has more services. Food in Carchi includes hearty soups, such as locro de papas, potato soup with cheese and avocado, as well as cuy, roasted guinea pig, and fritada, fried pork. Hot drinks help against the cold. Visit the cave shrine at La Paz, then ride into the páramo of El Ángel to see the frailejones; standing among them, in the mist, with the wind blowing, is an unforgettable experience.
t.segment loma virgen chiquito@0.5,-78.1:
High in the Andes of northern Ecuador, between El Ángel and Pimampiro in the province of Carchi, a stretch of the Qhapaq Ñan, the great road network of the Inca Empire, crosses the páramo, the high grassland that blankets the mountains above the tree line. The Inca built more than thirty thousand kilometres of roads across their empire, from Colombia to Chile and Argentina, linking towns, temples and storehouses, and this northern section, near the empire's frontier, was among the last to be built before the Spanish conquest. The Qhapaq Ñan was inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2014 as a transnational site shared by six countries, with hundreds of individual segments, including this one.

The páramo here is extraordinary. The El Ángel Ecological Reserve, nearby, protects a landscape dominated by frailejones, strange plants with tall, furry stems and rosettes of silvery leaves that look like something from another planet. These plants thrive in the cold, wet conditions of the high Andes, at elevations around 3,500 to 4,000 metres, and they act like sponges, capturing moisture from the mist and feeding the rivers that flow down to the valleys. Andean condors, spectacled bears and deer live in the area, though sightings are rare.

Riding in this region is an adventure. The Pan-American Highway, running through the valleys, is generally in good condition but carries heavy traffic, including trucks and buses. The roads up into the páramo are narrow, often cobbled or unpaved, and become muddy and slippery in the rain, which is frequent. Altitude affects both rider and machine: engines lose power, and riders can suffer from altitude sickness, so take it slow. Weather changes quickly, with cold, rain and fog common even on sunny days, so carry warm and waterproof gear.

El Ángel, a small town about seventeen kilometres away, has basic services, including fuel and simple restaurants, and Ibarra, a city of over a hundred thousand people, has everything. Local food includes hearty soups, potatoes, corn and grilled meats, along with fresh cheese from the highland dairies. Ride up to the páramo early in the day, when the weather is often clearer, and walk among the frailejones. The silence, the cold air and the strange plants make it an unforgettable experience.
t.san pedro de la roca castle@20.0,-75.9:
Where the narrow mouth of Santiago de Cuba's bay meets the open Caribbean, a castle climbs the headland in terraces of stone. San Pedro de la Roca, often called simply El Morro, was designed in the seventeenth century by the Italian military engineer Giovanni Battista Antonelli, from a family that built defences across the Spanish Caribbean. It was meant to shut the door on the pirates and privateers who had sacked Santiago more than once, and its tiered batteries, drawbridges and stairs follow the rock so closely that the fortress seems carved from it. It became a World Heritage Site in 1997 as the best preserved example of Spanish-American military architecture of its type.

From the ramparts you look across a blue bay and the green slopes of the Sierra Maestra to the west, while below the cliffs the swell surges into rocky inlets. Sunset is the time to be there, when a ceremony with costumed soldiers fires a cannon and the light goes amber over the water.

Santiago itself is the most Caribbean of Cuban cities: hot, hilly and musical, the home of son, with the Casa de la Trova in the centre where bands play from the afternoon on. It was here in 1953 that Fidel Castro led the attack on the Moncada barracks, and the city takes its revolutionary history seriously. Its carnival in July is one of the loudest in the Caribbean. Twelve kilometres west, the basilica of El Cobre houses the Virgin of Charity, patron saint of Cuba, and sits beside an old copper mine.

Riding in eastern Cuba is a real adventure. The coastal road west from Santiago towards Chivirico and Pilón runs between mountains and sea and is one of the most spectacular in the country, but storms have repeatedly damaged it, so expect potholes, washed-out sections and gravel. Traffic is light but includes horse carts, trucks with people in the back and dogs asleep on the asphalt. The heat is serious all year, and from June to November hurricane season adds a layer of uncertainty.

Fuel shortages are a recurring problem in Cuba, and stations may run dry or limit purchases, so fill whenever you can in Santiago and carry a reserve. The city has workshops of great ingenuity, used to keeping very old vehicles alive.
The hills around Marsella, in Risaralda, are steep enough that you wonder how anyone harvests coffee on them at all, and the answer is by hand, bean by bean, on slopes where the pickers lean into the hillside. This is the heart of Colombia's coffee region, the Eje Cafetero, and the cultural landscape of coffee growing here was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2011. The listing covers farms, towns and the traditions of a culture built around a crop that has shaped the country's history and identity.

The coffee farms, or fincas, are typically small, family-run and planted with coffee bushes shaded by banana plants, guadua bamboo and other trees. The towns, founded by settlers from Antioquia in the nineteenth century, have colourful houses with wooden balconies, central squares with churches and cafés where farmers gather. Marsella, seven kilometres away, is a charming example, with a botanical garden and a particularly beautiful cemetery set on a hillside.

The landscape is green, lush and spectacular, with mountains, valleys and rivers. The climate is mild, with two rainy seasons a year, roughly from April to May and from October to November. Rain often comes in heavy afternoon showers, and roads can be affected by landslides. The altitude, typically between 1,000 and 2,000 metres, keeps temperatures pleasant.

Riding in the coffee region is wonderful but demanding. Roads are steep and winding, with tight hairpins, narrow sections and occasional unpaved stretches. Traffic includes buses, trucks and the famous Willys jeeps, which are used to transport coffee and people. Be prepared for sudden rain, mud on the road and slow-moving vehicles. The scenery is worth it: every bend reveals new views of coffee plantations, forests and mountains.

Pereira, twelve kilometres away, is a large city with all services, and Marsella has fuel and shops. Coffee is, of course, everywhere, and many fincas offer tours explaining the process from bean to cup. The hot springs of Santa Rosa de Cabal, near Pereira, are a great place to relax after a day's ride. Try bandeja paisa, a huge plate of beans, rice, meat, egg, plantain and arepa, if you are really hungry.

Tulcán is the last Ecuadorian city before Colombia, a high, cold, windswept place at almost 3,000 metres, and it has one of the strangest sights in the Andes: a cemetery where cypress trees have been clipped into elaborate topiary, with figures, arches and geometric shapes, a tradition started by a local gardener in the 1930s. Near the city, the segment of Inca road between Pulcas and Troya is part of the Qhapaq Ñan World Heritage Site, marking the northern reaches of the Inca road system, which extended into what is now southern Colombia.

The Inca conquered this region late, in the early sixteenth century, shortly before the arrival of the Spanish. The Pasto people who lived here resisted fiercely, and the road represented the expansion of Inca power to the very edge of their empire. Today traces of the road can be found in the fields and hills, often used by farmers and herders.

The landscape is high Andean, with green fields, pastures and the páramo, a high-altitude grassland with frailejones, tall plants with woolly leaves that look like something from another planet. The El Ángel Ecological Reserve, south of Tulcán, protects a large area of páramo, and the roads through it offer stunning views. The weather is cold and often wet, with fog and drizzle.

Riding here is cold, high and beautiful. The Pan-American Highway crosses the border at Rumichaca, and the roads around Tulcán are winding and steep, with buses, trucks and border traffic. Across the border in Colombia, the Sanctuary of Las Lajas, a neo-Gothic church built across a gorge, is a spectacular sight and only a short ride away. Bring warm clothes and rain gear.

Tulcán, eight kilometres away, has fuel and everything else a border city offers, and Ipiales on the Colombian side is just as well supplied. Fuel prices differ sharply between the two countries, which explains the jerry cans you will see changing hands. Border crossings require the usual paperwork for vehicles, so make sure your documents are in order before setting out.
t.inantaz@1.1,-77.4:
Tangua and Yacuanquer are small highland towns in the department of Nariño, in the far south-west of Colombia, and Inantaz sits among their fields at roughly the latitude of the equator, on high ground above the valley of the Guáitara. This is the Andean altiplano of Nariño, a patchwork of potato, maize and pasture fields on steep slopes, with volcanoes rising behind. Galeras, the active volcano above Pasto, is not far to the north-east, and on a clear morning its cone dominates the view.

The roads in this region are demanding and beautiful. The Pan-American highway climbs and drops through the Andes with long bends and a mix of heavy lorries and small buses, so the pace is uneven. Side roads between Tangua and Yacuanquer are narrower, often with potholes and sudden gravel patches, and cattle or dogs can appear around any corner. Rain is frequent, especially in the afternoon, and mist often fills the valleys before noon. If you start early, you get cool air, sharp light and a road that smells of damp earth and woodsmoke.

Nariño has a distinct culture. The Pasto people, who lived here before the Incas and the Spanish, were known for farming steep land and for a fierce resistance to the early conquerors. Today the region is known for a local carnival, the Blacks and Whites carnival in Pasto in early January, which UNESCO recognised as intangible heritage, and for handicrafts such as barniz de Pasto, a decorative technique using a vegetable resin to inlay wood. Guinea pig, cuy, is a regional dish for celebrations, and people here often eat it roasted whole.

For fuel, do not rely on the small villages. The larger town in the data is Guaitarilla, but the main city in the area is Pasto, which has a full range of services, and Ipiales to the south is a good choice for the border region. Keep your tank healthy and carry some cash, since not every small shop takes cards. Altitude here is considerable, often above two and a half thousand metres, so the engine feels a little flat and you will notice the cold at dusk. A wool layer under your jacket is no luxury.
t.san pedro@0.8,-77.5:
Ipiales is the last big Colombian town before Ecuador, and the high, cold plateau around it is some of the most dramatic farmland in the Andes. San Pedro lies a little north-west of the city, in a landscape of terraces, small farms and green slopes that tilt toward the canyon of the Guáitara river. The land is at about 2,900 metres and above, so mornings begin with frost on the grass and a hard blue sky.

Ipiales is better known for the Las Lajas sanctuary, a neo-Gothic church built across the gorge of the Guáitara, so that the structure seems to hang from the cliff. It was built in the first half of the twentieth century on the site of an older shrine, and it is one of the most photographed churches in South America. It is a few kilometres from the city, and if you are in the area, you should go. It is crowded on weekends, and quiet and moody in a drizzle.

The ride is demanding. Roads climb and drop, the surface is a patchwork of asphalt and repairs, and heavy lorries on the Pan-American highway can make overtaking tense. Small lanes between the villages are less busy but have potholes and drainage cuts. Weather swings between sun and cold rain quickly, so a waterproof layer is a necessity, and the light, when the cloud lifts, is sharp and gorgeous. It is a landscape that rewards slow riding.

Ipiales has seventy-seven thousand people, so it has everything: fuel, food, workshops and hotels. In the small settlements, you cannot count on any of that. Buy your fuel in the city and take cash. Altitude affects the engine, with carburetted bikes running rich, so a slightly flat feel is normal. The border with Ecuador at Rumichaca is only a few minutes beyond, and the crossing is busy with trucks, so check the paperwork for your bike in advance if you plan to continue.

For food, try a plate of local potatoes with cheese, a hot soup called locro, or a bowl of hot chocolate with a piece of cheese in it, a Colombian habit that sounds odd until you try it on a cold morning. The hills here are green most of the year, and the air has a slightly smoky, sweet smell from farm fires.
t.dos palmas contramaestre@20.0,-76.1:
Eastern Cuba has a very different feel from Havana, and the country between Santiago and Palma Soriano shows why. This is the foothill country of the Sierra Maestra, the mountain range where the revolution began in the 1950s, and the land is a mix of cane fields, mango and royal palm, small farms and steep green ridges to the south. Dos Palmas is the name of a locality here, close to El Cobre, home of the great copper-domed basilica where the Virgin of Charity is venerated, and Palma Soriano, the main town of the valley.

El Cobre takes its name from the copper mines that the Spanish worked here from the sixteenth century, using enslaved Africans and later free labour, and the basilica commemorates the miraculous little statue found floating in the bay of Nipe, according to tradition. Pilgrims from across the island make their way here, and Ernest Hemingway famously left his Nobel medal at the shrine for a time. The rest of the valley carries traces of the same history, with old sugar mills, rusting railway lines and slowly decaying colonial houses.

Riding in Cuba is its own adventure, and in this region you should expect a modest, sometimes rough surface. The Carretera Central, the main national road, runs through the region as a two-lane highway with a patched surface, horse carts, bicycles, old American cars, tractors, and now and then a cow. Potholes can be deep and are not always marked, so keep your speed down and watch the edges. After dark, the lack of lighting makes things much harder, so aim to be off the road before sunset. The dry season from December to April is the most comfortable time. From June to October brings heavy rain, humidity and the risk of hurricanes.

Practical matters need real thought. Fuel supply in Cuba has been unreliable in recent years, with queues and shortages, so do not count on filling up where you want. Palma Soriano, a town of about a hundred thousand, is the largest nearby place for services, and Santiago de Cuba is bigger still. Carry water and cash in small notes, and expect to pay for a coffee or a plate of rice, beans and pork at a private home with a smile.

The Valle del Cauca is one of the richest farmland regions of Colombia, a wide, flat valley between two great ranges of the Andes, and this point lies on its western edge, where the plain begins to climb into the mountains. The Cauca river runs through the middle, and on either side lie fields of sugar cane in a green sea that stretches for kilometres, harvested for most of the year, with columns of smoke and cane trucks on the roads. The Western Cordillera rises to the west, covered in cloud forest, and its slopes hold coffee farms, small villages and some of the best birdwatching in South America.

The nearest settlements tell the story of the region. Trujillo and Riofrío are small, friendly towns of a few thousand people, with plazas, churches and shops, and Tuluá, a city of more than a hundred and sixty thousand, lies down in the valley with its markets, fuel stations and food. The region was once the territory of the Calima people, who made gold ornaments of astonishing delicacy, and the nearby Calima lake, formed by a dam, is now a magnet for windsurfers and kitesurfers, who come for the steady wind.

Riding in Colombia is an education. Motorbikes are everywhere, carrying families, goods and cooking gas, and car drivers are used to them, but overtaking is bold and traffic can be chaotic near towns. The main roads are good, wide and well signed, with toll booths where motorbikes pay a reduced fare, and the mountain roads are twisty, steep and scenic, with sudden fog in the higher sections. Landslides are a risk in the rainy seasons, from April to May and October to November.

Fuel is easy in Tuluá and available in the larger villages, and you will find roadside stalls selling fresh fruit, coffee and fried snacks. Try sancocho, the hearty soup of chicken or beef with plantain and yuca, and finish with a cup of local coffee. Afternoons are hot in the valley, and cooler up in the hills, so carry a light jacket. The dry months, from June to September and December to February, are the best for riding, and the valley's green is most striking after rain.
t.buffalo@42.9,-78.9:
Buffalo sits at the east end of Lake Erie, where the lake narrows into the Niagara River, and its position has shaped everything about it. The Erie Canal ended here when it opened in 1825, linking the Great Lakes to the Hudson and New York, and the city became a great grain port, its waterfront crowded with huge concrete elevators, many of which still stand. At one point in the early twentieth century it was among the richest cities in America, and the legacy is still visible in its architecture, from the art deco city hall to the Frank Lloyd Wright houses.

Today Buffalo has about a quarter of a million people, a revived waterfront, and a deserved reputation for friendliness and good food. It claims the chicken wing, which was supposedly invented at a bar here in the 1960s, and beef on weck, a roast-beef sandwich on a salted roll, is a local speciality. Fuel and food are plentiful, and the city's old neighbourhoods have good bakeries and diners. The Peace Bridge, across the Niagara River to Canada, is a short ride away, and Niagara Falls lies about thirty minutes north.

For a rider, the Seaway Trail, which follows the lake and river shorelines for hundreds of miles, begins or ends here, passing vineyards, orchards, small harbours and lighthouses. The roads are flat and gentle, with occasional lake views, and there is a pleasant ride along the lakeshore through the old resort towns. Traffic in the city is typical, with rush-hour jams on the expressways, but the back roads are quiet.

Weather is the character. Lake Erie's influence is huge: winters bring lake-effect snow in great storms, summers are mild, and the lake keeps the autumn warm. The best months for riding are June to September. Sunsets over the lake can be spectacular, and a walk along the waterfront at dusk, with ships moving slowly across the horizon, is a fine way to finish a day. Give yourself time to see the grain elevators and the old canal terminus.
t.pittsburgh@40.4,-80.0:
Pittsburgh makes sense once you see where it sits. The city grew at the meeting of the Allegheny and Monongahela rivers, which merge to form the Ohio, and the point where they meet is now a park with a fountain at the tip. Steep hills rise from the water on every side, and the streets climb them in flights of stairs, so that the old neighbourhoods look stacked on one another. More than four hundred bridges cross the rivers and ravines, and it is the sort of city where you cross a bridge without noticing.

Riders arriving from the south get the best welcome of all. The Fort Pitt Tunnel carries the highway under Mount Washington, and as you come out of its mouth, the whole downtown spreads out in front of you across the rivers, with the bridges gleaming. It is one of the great urban reveals in America. The Duquesne Incline, a cable car from the 1870s, still climbs the same hill, and the view from the top at dusk is worth the fare.

Steel once defined the city, and the old mills lined the rivers, belching smoke, but the economy has since turned to medicine, education and technology. The Cathedral of Learning, a forty-two storey Gothic tower belonging to the university, is a landmark of the Oakland district. t.fort henry@44.2,-76.5:

t.cathcart tower@44.2,-76.5:

t.fort frederick@44.2,-76.5:

t.delaware water gap@41.0,-75.1:

t.cape vincent@44.1,-76.3:

t.warren@41.8,-79.1:

t.frenchtown@40.5,-75.1:

t.milford new jersey@40.6,-75.1:

t.nevado del ruiz@4.9,-75.3:

t.cali@3.5,-76.5:

t.san agustin colombia@1.9,-76.3:

t.las lajas@0.8,-77.6:

t.laguna de la cocha@1.1,-77.1:

t.otavalo@0.2,-78.3:

t.ibarra@0.4,-78.1:

t.tulcan@0.8,-77.7:

t.el angel@0.6,-77.9:

Wind is constant, so go early, wear warm gloves, and prepare for rain. Drive slowly, because cattle often graze near the road.

Higher up, the reserve holds lakes, including the Lagunas del Voladero, with clear water and a boardwalk across the wetlands, and tufts of cushion plants that store water like sponges. Birds of prey circle overhead, and with luck you may see a spectacled bear, a puma or an Andean fox, though they are shy. The plants themselves grow only a few centimetres a year, so some of the oldest are many decades old, and visitors are asked to keep to the paths.

Fuel is the point to plan around. San Gabriel is also a good place for a warm lunch, with simple restaurants serving hearty soups, and a morning market. If you are staying overnight, there are small guesthouses, and evenings are very cold, so carry a warm layer and keep your bike covered. The park office gives current information about conditions.
t.segment piman caranqui@0.4,-78.1:
Ibarra sits in a high basin in northern Ecuador at around 2,200 metres, beneath the green slopes of Imbabura volcano, and the Inca road ran right through this valley. The Qhapaq Ñan, the Andean road system, stretched over 30,000 kilometres from Colombia to Chile and Argentina, linking the Inca empire, and it was inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2014. The segment between Pimán and Caranqui is one of the preserved sections in Ecuador, a stretch of old path through farmland and hills, with dry-stone edging in places and the kind of steady, sensible gradient Inca engineers favoured for runners and llama trains. Caranqui, now a suburb of Ibarra, was an important Inca centre, and local tradition claims it as the birthplace of Atahualpa, the last Inca emperor.

Ibarra is known as the white city, for its whitewashed colonial buildings, and it was largely rebuilt after an earthquake destroyed it in 1868. It is a pleasant, laid-back town with fuel, shops, restaurants and hotels. Try the helados de paila, sorbet churned in a copper pan over ice, a local specialty.

North of the town, Yahuarcocha, the lake of blood, is named after a battle in which the Inca are said to have massacred the Caranqui people. Today, it has a motor racing circuit around the lake. To the south, the town of Otavalo hosts one of the largest indigenous markets in South America, and the Andean landscape around it, with volcanoes, lakes and patchwork fields, is spectacular.

Riding here is a mix of good highways, like the Pan-American, and rough, steep cobbled or dirt roads into the hills. Altitude affects both rider and machine, and weather can change quickly, with rain and fog in the afternoon. Watch for buses, trucks, dogs and livestock. The dry season, roughly June to September, is the best time to ride, and mornings usually offer the clearest views of the volcanoes.
t.el salvador@20.3,-75.3:
In the mountains north of Guantánamo, at the eastern end of Cuba, the Sierra del Purial and the hills around the town of El Salvador rise steeply from the dry coastal plain into a greener, cooler world of forest and coffee. At the end of the eighteenth century, French planters fleeing the slave revolution in Saint-Domingue, today's Haiti, settled in these mountains and built coffee plantations, with stone drying terraces, mills, aqueducts and grand houses, worked by enslaved Africans. The ruins of more than a hundred and seventy of these plantations survive in the Sierra Maestra and around Guantánamo, and they were listed by UNESCO in 2000 as the Archaeological Landscape of the First Coffee Plantations in the South-East of Cuba.

Many of the plantations are now overgrown, their stone walls and terraces swallowed by the forest, but walking among them you can still see the scale of the enterprise and the cleverness of the engineering, with water channels and drying floors carved into the slopes. The region's history is complex and painful, marked by slavery, revolution and the long presence of the United States naval base at Guantánamo Bay, which you may see from a distance. To the east, the Alejandro de Humboldt National Park protects one of the richest rainforests in the Caribbean, with many endemic species.

Riding in eastern Cuba is an adventure. Roads range from decent tarmac to potholed tracks, with horse-drawn carts, bicycles, trucks and pedestrians all sharing the space. Signage is limited, and night riding is risky due to poor lighting and unexpected obstacles. The road to Baracoa over the mountains, La Farola, is one of the most famous in Cuba, with hairpins, viewpoints and roadside stalls selling cucurucho, a sweet made of coconut wrapped in a palm leaf cone.

Fuel can be hard to find in Cuba, with frequent shortages, so fill up whenever possible in larger towns like Guantánamo and carry extra if you can. Food in the countryside is simple: rice and beans, pork, plantains and fresh fruit. Bring water, sun protection and patience, and be prepared for heat and sudden tropical storms, especially from June to November.
t.niceto perez@20.1,-75.3:
Niceto Pérez is a rural municipality in the hills just west of the city of Guantánamo, in the far east of Cuba, a region of sugar cane, small farms and mountains rising towards the Sierra Maestra and the coffee country of the Gran Piedra. It is not a place that features in many guidebooks, and that is part of its interest. The surrounding hills hold the remains of the coffee plantations established in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries by French planters fleeing the revolution in Saint-Domingue, now Haiti, and the archaeological landscape of those first coffee plantations in the south east of Cuba is listed by UNESCO.

The French brought with them knowledge, capital and enslaved Africans, and they built a remarkable system of terraced plantations, drying platforms, aqueducts and houses on the steep slopes of the eastern mountains. Many of the plantations were abandoned in the nineteenth century, and their ruins now lie hidden in the forest, slowly being reclaimed by nature. The most famous, the Cafetal La Isabelica, near the Gran Piedra above Santiago de Cuba, has been restored as a museum.

Guantánamo, about twelve kilometres away, is the main city of the province, with a population of more than two hundred thousand. It gave its name to one of the most famous Cuban songs, Guantanamera, and it is the birthplace of changüí, a style of music that is a forerunner of son and salsa. The nearby American naval base, at the bay of Guantánamo, is off limits, but there are viewpoints from which you can see it in the distance.

Riding in eastern Cuba is an adventure. The roads vary from reasonable to very poor, with potholes, broken surfaces and unexpected obstacles, including horse-drawn carts, cyclists, pedestrians and livestock. Fuel can be hard to find, with shortages common in recent years, so fill up whenever you can and carry spare fuel if possible. The heat and humidity are intense, especially in summer, and the hurricane season runs from June to November. Water and food supplies are limited in rural areas, so plan carefully, carry supplies, and ask local people for advice. Their hospitality is one of the great rewards of travelling in Cuba.
t.rosal de chapal@0.9,-77.4:
High in the department of Nariño, in Colombia's far southwest, the land folds into deep canyons cut by the Guáitara River, and the old Inca road, the Qhapaq Ñan, threads along the slopes. Rosal de Chapal is one of the surviving fragments of that road on the Colombian side, a stretch of track near the small towns of Funes, Iles and Contadero. The Qhapaq Ñan, a network of roads that tied the Inca empire together from present day Colombia to Chile and Argentina, was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2014, and Nariño holds its northernmost sections.

It is easy to underestimate how high you are. These are the Andes at around three thousand metres, with cold mornings, strong sun and air that saps energy on a walk. The fields are a patchwork of potatoes, barley and pasture climbing improbably steep slopes, with eucalyptus windbreaks and adobe houses. Clouds boil up from the canyons in the afternoon, and rain can turn dirt tracks to grease fast.

The riding here is serious. Main roads in Nariño are paved but busy with trucks and buses, with sharp bends, landslide scars and sudden potholes, while the side roads toward the canyon villages are often unpaved, steep and rutted. A light bike and good tyres make sense, and so does riding in daylight only. The descent into the Guáitara gorge and the climb out again are spectacular, but give them time.

Not far south, the sanctuary of Las Lajas near Ipiales is built across the Guáitara canyon itself, a neo-Gothic church on a bridge over the river, and it is one of the great sights of southern Colombia. Funes is known for its canyon and for the road between Pasto and Ipiales passing through the region. Local food runs to hearty soups, roast guinea pig, cuy, which is a regional speciality, and hot drinks to fight off the chill.

Funes and Iles are small towns of a couple of thousand people with shops but limited services; do not count on fuel there. Pupiales, about twenty kilometres away, and especially Ipiales or Pasto are where to fill up and find reliable food and lodging. Carry water, warm layers and a rain cover, and check local advice on road conditions before heading down any canyon track.
t.segment rumichaca@0.8,-77.7:
Rumichaca means stone bridge in Quechua, and the name is literal: here the Carchi River, which becomes the Guáitara on the Colombian side, flows beneath a natural arch of rock that has carried travellers between what are now Colombia and Ecuador for centuries. The Inca road passed this way, and a segment of the Qhapaq Ñan near the crossing is part of the World Heritage listing. Today the main border post between the two countries sits right here, with the modern bridge carrying the Pan-American Highway beside the old crossing.

Ipiales, three kilometres away, is the Colombian border city, a busy, chilly place at close to three thousand metres with markets, money changers and bus terminals. On the Ecuadorian side, Tulcán is famous for its cemetery, where cypress hedges have been clipped into extraordinary topiary figures, and it is worth an hour if you are crossing. Both towns are working towns rather than pretty ones, but they have everything a traveller needs.

For riders the main thing here is paperwork. Crossing with a vehicle means temporary import documents, passport stamps, and insurance requirements on each side, and the queues can be long, especially around holidays. Arrive early in the day, have copies of everything, and be patient. Fuel prices differ noticeably between the two countries, which is why you will see people filling cans; follow the rules and do not carry fuel across.

The road itself is the Pan-American, paved, high and often misty, with heavy trucks grinding up and down. North toward Pasto it winds through the Andes with long climbs and deep valleys; south into Ecuador it heads toward the páramo grasslands and the Ecuadorian highlands. Wet weather is common, and visibility can drop to a few metres in cloud. Ride with lights on and expect animals and pedestrians on the shoulder.

Nearby, the Las Lajas sanctuary, built on a bridge over the Guáitara gorge a short ride from Ipiales, is the essential detour. Pupiales, a small town to the northwest, is quieter than Ipiales. Ipiales has the most reliable fuel, food and lodging on the Colombian side, Tulcán on the Ecuadorian side. Dress warmly; even on a sunny day the wind at the border bites.
t.la cofradia@0.9,-77.6:
Down in Colombia's far south, close to the border with Ecuador, the Andes spread into a high, rumpled plateau of small fields stitched together by hedges, with deep canyons cut into it by rivers rushing towards the Pacific and the Amazon. La Cofradía lies here in the department of Nariño, between Gualmatán and Contadero, at the height of the old Inca road network, the Qhapaq Ñan, which reached this far north as the empire's frontier pushed into what is now Colombia. A few stretches of the road around here are part of the Qhapaq Ñan World Heritage site.

At around three thousand metres, the air is thin and cool, and the light is sharp. The landscape is a patchwork of potato fields, pastures and eucalyptus groves, with farmhouses and small villages scattered across the slopes. Cloud often sits on the ridges in the afternoon, and rain can come at any time of year. Mornings tend to be clearest, so get going early if you want the views.

The riding is challenging and rewarding. The Pan-American Highway runs from Pasto south to Ipiales and the border, a road with many curves, climbs and descents, but also heavy truck traffic and sections under repair. Off the main road, the routes through villages like Gualmatán and Contadero are narrow, steep and often unpaved, with tight bends and spectacular views into the Guáitara canyon. Watch for landslides after rain, animals on the road and local drivers overtaking in surprising places.

Just south, near Ipiales, the Sanctuary of Las Lajas is one of the most extraordinary churches in the world, a neo-Gothic basilica built on a bridge spanning the Guáitara canyon, with the river roaring below. It is a major pilgrimage site, and the setting alone is worth the detour. Nariño's people are proud of their indigenous heritage, and markets in the towns are full of colourful textiles, potatoes of many varieties, and guinea pig, known as cuy, roasted whole on a spit.

Pupiales, about nine kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size with fuel and food. Ipiales, a larger border town, has more options. Make sure you have cash, as card payment is not always available, and dress warmly; the evenings at this altitude are cold, even near the equator.
t.el cobre@20.1,-75.9:
Few places in Cuba matter as much to ordinary people as the little town of El Cobre, high on a hill about thirteen kilometres west of Santiago de Cuba. Its basilica, a yellow-and-white church with three domes standing against the green of the Sierra Maestra, holds the Virgen de la Caridad del Cobre, the patron saint of Cuba, a small statue of the Virgin dressed in gold. Believers and non-believers alike treat her as a symbol of the nation, and the pilgrimage on her feast day, the eighth of September, draws crowds from across the island.

The story goes that three men out in a boat in the Bay of Nipe, in the early seventeenth century, found the statue floating on a plank on the water, and she was brought to the copper mines at El Cobre, from which the town takes its name. The mines were among the earliest in the Americas, and they were worked by enslaved Africans, some of whom escaped and fought for their freedom. A monument to the cimarrón, the runaway slave, stands on a hilltop outside the town, reached by steps and giving a wide view over the hills. Ernest Hemingway gave his Nobel medal to the shrine in 1954, and visitors leave offerings of every kind in the chapel, from candles to small copper models of limbs.

The ride from Santiago is short but characterful. The road climbs from the coastal plain into the foothills with some curves, with potholes and loose patches, and animals and bicycles on the road. Always keep an eye out for horse carts, cyclists and unlit vehicles at dusk. The best time to travel is the dry season, from November to April, and it is better to come early in the morning before the heat builds and the pilgrim crowds arrive. The sea is within easy reach, and the fort at San Pedro de la Roca, on the cliffs at the mouth of Santiago Bay, is a good addition to the same day.

Fuel in Cuba is a changeable matter, and you should not count on it. Santiago, with more than half a million people, is the place to look, and it is wise to ask locally before you set out. El Cobre has small shops and stalls and a few places for coffee and sandwiches, and Santiago has the livelier, smoky bars and music that the east of Cuba is known for.
t.zone d@4.6,-75.7:
Armenia, Colombia, is not the best-known part of the country, but the hills around it are the heart of the Eje Cafetero, the coffee axis. The Coffee Cultural Landscape of Colombia is a UNESCO World Heritage Site made up of several zones, and Zone D lies in Quindío, in the high green country close to Armenia, Circasia and Montenegro. This is where the coffee farms cling to steep slopes, shaded by plantain and tall guadua bamboo, and the farmhouses are painted in bright colours with carved balconies.

The landscape is a patchwork of small family farms that have grown coffee for generations, and the local culture is proud and welcoming. In Armenia, the old Willys jeeps, loaded with sacks and passengers, are a symbol, and they parade every year in the Yipao festival. A short ride away, the Parque Nacional del Café in Montenegro and the town of Salento, near the Cocora Valley with its towering wax palms, draw many visitors. Coffee itself is everywhere, served black, strong and sweet.

Armenia is a city of over three hundred thousand, with fuel, workshops and plenty of places to eat, and it was rebuilt after a powerful earthquake in January 1999 that devastated the region. The hills around have excellent riding roads, with long climbs and descents, tight bends and views over valleys full of coffee bushes and banana leaves. The surface is generally paved, but watch for potholes, landslide debris and heavy trucks. The weather is usually warm, with afternoon rain, and the roads can be slick.

The main rainy seasons are April to May and October to November, and the drier months from December to March offer the clearest views. Mornings are cool and misty, and the light across the hills is soft and gold. Stay at a working finca if you can, tour the plantation and taste a freshly roasted cup. The food, from bandeja paisa to fresh trout and arepas, is hearty and filling.
t.rumichaca@0.8,-77.6:
The border between Colombia and Ecuador crosses a gorge, and for centuries people have crossed it on a natural stone bridge. Rumichaca, from Quechua for stone bridge, spans the Carchi river a few kilometres from Ipiales, and it was an Inca route long before the modern frontier existed. Today it is a busy international crossing, with a customs complex on the Colombian side and the city of Tulcán waiting on the Ecuadorian side, and the old rock arch sits in a small park among the buildings, easy to miss amid the lorries.

The land here is high, cold and green. Ipiales sits near three thousand metres above the sea, in the Andean highlands of Nariño, a land of potato fields, potreros with dairy cows, and misty páramo above. Nights are chilly even in the dry season, and the weather can swing from sun to drizzle in an hour. A few kilometres from town, the Sanctuary of Las Lajas, a neo-Gothic basilica built across a river canyon in the twentieth century, is one of the most photographed churches in the country, and it should not be missed.

Riders heading south on the Pan-American Highway will pass through here, and the border formalities take planning. You will need your passport, vehicle papers and insurance, and possibly a temporary import permit, so allow several hours and check current rules in advance. Ipiales, three kilometres away, has fuel, restaurants and money changers, and it is the sensible place to prepare before crossing. Tulcán, in Ecuador, is known for its cemetery, where cypress hedges are clipped into archways and figures.

The road itself is a good paved highway with trucks, long curves and fast, mountainous scenery, though fog and rain make visibility poor in the afternoon. Wear layers, because the altitude chills you quickly, and take care on wet surfaces. Ipiales has cuy, roasted guinea pig, on some menus, and a hot canelazo, a cinnamon and aguardiente drink, goes down well after a cold ride.
t.los ajos@1.1,-77.3:
Pasto sits at the foot of Galeras, an active volcano of more than 4,200 metres that has rumbled and smoked on and off for centuries, and the farm country around it lies in the shadow of that mountain. Los Ajos is a rural spot in this southern Colombian highland, in the department of Nariño, a few kilometres from the small towns of Yacuanquer and Tangua.

Riding in Nariño is cool, high and sometimes wet. The roads climb through the Andes in tight bends, with fog patches and surprise stretches of broken asphalt, and mornings tend to be the clearest. Altitude is substantial, so bring a warm jacket and a waterproof layer even in the dry months of July and August. Heavy trucks use the main roads between Pasto and the Ecuadorian border, so overtaking needs patience, and landslides after rain can close sections, so check road conditions before you go.

Pasto, a city of nearly four hundred thousand people about twelve kilometres away, is where you buy fuel, supplies and a proper meal. It is known for a remarkable carnival, held in early January, the Carnival of Blacks and Whites, which UNESCO recognises as intangible heritage, and for a decorative craft in which artisans cover wood with resin from a local plant to produce brightly coloured designs. In the restaurants look for cuy, roast guinea pig, which is a highland tradition and a matter of local pride.

Further south the road runs on toward Ipiales, with its neo-Gothic church built across a river canyon, the Las Lajas sanctuary, which is among the most striking pilgrimage sites in South America. Even if you do not make the detour, the sight of the volcano on a clear morning, lit pink and white above the farms, is worth the early start.
t.guapuscal bajo@1.1,-77.4:
The Andes of southern Colombia look folded rather than carved, a series of green ridges one behind another until the cloud hides them, and Guapuscal Bajo sits in the middle of that country. The name means lower Guapuscal, which implies an upper one higher up the slope, and the pair are small farming settlements in the municipality of Tangua, in the department of Nariño. There is no famous landmark to point to here. The interest lies in the day-to-day landscape, in small terraced plots of potatoes, onions, maize and pasture, in the kids in uniform walking the lanes and the smoke rising from kitchen stoves.

On a motorcycle this is real highland riding. The roads rise and fall in short, steep sections, often narrow, with sudden changes from smooth asphalt to gravel or concrete strips laid by the local council. Expect farm animals, motorbike taxis and slow-moving trucks, and give yourself plenty of time. The climate is cool and changeable, and fog is common at higher elevations, so visibility can drop quickly. Mornings are best, and the rainy seasons, roughly from October to December and again in spring, make many side roads slippery.

Tangua and Funes are the nearest villages, each with a couple of thousand people, and both have small shops and places to eat a plain, filling lunch. For fuel, do not rely on villages this size. Guaitarilla, about seventeen kilometres away, is a larger town, and Pasto, the departmental capital, is the dependable stop with stations, workshops and hotels. Fill up before you leave the main road rather than hoping for a pump up the hill.

What you will carry away is mostly the feel of the place, the sound of cowbells and rushing water, the cold at dawn, the smell of woodsmoke and wet earth, and the generosity of people who often wave at a passing rider. Greet them in Spanish, accept a coffee if it is offered, and take your time on the bends.
t.segment juan montalvo cabuyal@0.6,-78.1:
Northern Ecuador is where the Andes narrow and the country almost touches Colombia, and this stretch between Juan Montalvo and Cabuyal lies in the highland province of Carchi, not far from the little town of El Ángel. The area sits in the shadow of the páramo, the cold, treeless grassland above the forest line, where frailejones, the tall, silvery, furry-leaved plants, stand like crowds of strange sentinels. The El Ángel Ecological Reserve, a short way off, protects a large stretch of this habitat, and on a cloudy day it feels like another planet.

The riding is rewarding and demanding. Mountain roads here climb steeply from the warm, dry Mira valley to cold plateaux above three thousand metres, with hairpin bends, patches of broken surface and the occasional cow on the carriageway. Mornings are usually clear, and by afternoon cloud rolls in and temperatures drop quickly, so pack waterproofs and a warm layer. Altitude can affect both rider and engine, and fuel stations get scarcer as you climb, so fill up before you leave Ibarra.

Ibarra, about twenty-six kilometres away, is the city to know, with more than a hundred thousand people. Called the White City for its colonial buildings, it lies beside Lake Yahuarcocha and below the great cones of Imbabura and Cotacachi, and it is the place for fuel, food and a bed. Try the local ice cream made in copper pans, called helado de paila, a speciality of the region. El Ángel is much smaller, so check your tank before leaving the main road.

North of here the highway runs on to Tulcán and the border at Rumichaca, and the whole region is a corridor of old trade between the Inca heartland and the north. People speak of the wind in the páramo as a living thing, and standing among the frailejones on a bright morning you can hear what they mean. Go slowly, and pause often to look.
t.segment campana pucara quitoloma@0.0,-78:
The equator runs across northern Ecuador, a short ride from Quito, and the hills east of the capital, around Cayambe, hold some of the most interesting ancient sites in the country. This segment of the Qhapaq Ñan, the Inca road network recognised by UNESCO, links the pucará at Campana and the hill of Quitoloma, and the word pucará means fortress in Quechua. The Inca extended their empire into this region late, in the decades before the Spanish conquest, and they met fierce resistance from the local peoples, the Caranquis, who fought from hilltop forts. The landscape bears the marks of those wars in earthworks, ramparts and ditches on the hills.

The setting is magnificent. Cayambe volcano, at about five thousand eight hundred metres, rises above the plain with a permanent cap of ice, and the equator crosses its southern flank, the only point on the line with year-round snow, while the grass-covered páramo below is dotted with horses, cattle and indigenous farmers. Mist forms and clears quickly, and the air is cold and thin. The area also has older sites, such as the pyramids at Cochasquí, built by the Quitu-Cara people a thousand years ago, which are very close and can be combined in one outing.

The roads are good by Andean standards. The Panamericana climbs and falls across the high plains with smooth curves, and the road from Quito to Cayambe is busy, with trucks and buses and flower farms, since Cayambe is one of the biggest rose-growing regions in the world. Side roads to the pucarás are cobbled or gravel and can be slippery in rain. Altitude brings cold, and wind is common, so warm layers are essential. The dry months from June to September are the most reliable, and the mornings are clearest.

Cayambe, twelve kilometres away, is a town of about twenty-seven thousand people, known for its biscuits, bizcochos, which are baked in wood ovens and eaten with local cheese and a cup of hot chocolate. It has fuel stations, supermarkets and restaurants. Quito, a city of historic beauty and a UNESCO centre, is about an hour south. Fill your tank before going to the hills, bring water and sun protection, since UV is strong at altitude, and be respectful of farms and community lands when exploring.
t.la paz@0.9,-77.5:
There are several places named La Paz in Colombia, and this one is a small settlement in the department of Nariño, near the town of Contadero, in the high country close to the Ecuadorian border. Nariño is the land of the Pastos, the indigenous people who farmed these cold uplands before the Inca arrived, and it lies on the Qhapaq Ñan, the Inca road system that UNESCO listed in 2014. The road here follows the route that ran north from Quito toward Pasto, crossing deep canyons and high plateaus, and the old Inca line is part of the story of a landscape where cultures have met and mixed for centuries.

This is an agricultural highland, green and chilly, with potato fields, pastures, dairy cattle and small farms in a patchwork on steep slopes, and the volcano Cumbal visible to the west on a clear day. The Guáitara river has cut a spectacular canyon through the area, and the sanctuary of Las Lajas, a neo-Gothic basilica built across the gorge on a bridge, lies near Ipiales, a short drive away. It was built in the twentieth century on the site of a shrine associated with a miracle, and it appears to rise from the rock itself.

The riding is excellent and a little demanding. The Panamericana, here Route 25, runs through the highlands in long climbs and drops, with a decent surface in places and patches of damage in others, and heavy trucks on their way to the Ecuador border. Fog, rain and cold are frequent, and the altitude, about 2,800 to 3,000 metres, makes the air thin. Security conditions in border regions can vary, so check the latest advice and travel in daylight. The drier months, from December to February and from July to August, are better.

Contadero, one kilometre away, is a small town of about sixteen hundred people, and Pupiales, eleven kilometres off, has fuel, a market and restaurants, while the larger city of Ipiales is a short ride on and is the base for visiting Las Lajas. Try a plate of cuy, a typical Nariño dish, or empanadas and hot chocolate with cheese. Carry your vehicle papers and passport, and be sure to check the rules for crossing into Ecuador before heading to the border.
t.segment pulcas troya b@0.8,-77.7:
Close to the Colombian border, at almost three thousand metres, the páramo above Tulcán is a cold, windy country of tussock grass and cloud. Tulcán, a town of over eighty thousand people, is the capital of Carchi province, and it sits at the very top of the northern Andes of Ecuador, within sight of the volcanoes that straddle the frontier. The air here is thin and cool, even at midday, and the rain is never far away.

This is part of the Qhapaq Ñan, the great Inca road network that ran for thousands of kilometres along the Andes, linking Cusco with Quito and beyond. Sections of the road across Ecuador were added to the World Heritage list in 2014, and the segment here, between Pulcas and Troya, is one of the pieces that remains. The Incas built the road with stone paving, drainage and retaining walls, and it served messengers, armies and llama caravans. Before the Incas, the northern Andes were home to a number of local peoples, including the Pasto, who lived on both sides of what is now the border.

Riding in the region is a cool and often damp business, so pack a waterproof layer. The Pan-American Highway runs along the Andean spine and is the main artery, a good road with long climbs and descents, and a lot of trucks on the way to the border at Rumichaca. Away from the highway, rural roads can be rough, with gravel and potholes, and fog or drizzle can reduce visibility. The upside is the sense of landscape, with ploughed fields climbing the slopes and the páramo above, and the pale ribbon of the road unfolding.

Tulcán has everything a traveller needs, with several fuel stations, hotels, restaurants and markets. It is also famous for its cemetery, where cypress hedges have been clipped into arches, animals and geometric figures, and it is a strange and beautiful place to visit. Local food is hearty, with potatoes, guinea pig for the adventurous, and hot soups against the cold. The Colombian town of Ipiales, with its dramatic neo-Gothic sanctuary built in a canyon, lies just over the border.

Morning is the best time, when the cloud is often clear and the volcanoes can be seen. Bring a warm layer and keep your passport handy.
t.rochester new york@43.2,-77.6:
Rochester rose on water power. The Genesee River drops ninety feet over High Falls in the middle of the city, and in the early nineteenth century the mills along the gorge ground so much wheat that it was called the Flour City, before the nickname changed to the Flower City, for its nurseries and lilacs. The Erie Canal crossed the river here on a stone aqueduct, and the city grew on the canal trade. Today, High Falls still tumbles through the downtown, lit at night, and the old mill buildings are being turned into apartments and cafes.

The city's other inheritance is invention. t.salento@4.6,-75.6:

t.cocora valley@4.6,-75.5:

t.rattlesnake point@43.5,-79.9:

t.mount nemo@43.4,-79.9:

t.forks of the credit@43.8,-79.9:

t.cataract@43.8,-80.0:

t.mutsamudu@-12.2,44.4:

t.domoni@-12.3,44.5:

t.pereira@4.8,-75.7:

t.itsandra@-11.7,43.3:

t.ntsudjini@-11.7,43.3:

t.moroni@-11.7,43.3:

t.ikoni@-11.7,43.2:
